title: Democrats eye ambitious Senate map that was once unthinkable as anti-Trump backlash grows
content: For weeks, top Democrats in Washington have watched with cautious restraint as Republicans dumped millions into red states like Kansas and South Carolina to defend an increasingly shaky Senate map. But Democrats increasingly believe they have a real chance to win seats deep in Trump territory as Republicans face their worst midterm environment in decades and the Senate map abruptly expands. Democrats are now adding Kansas to a growing list of unlikely targets as they also try to flip Texas, Alaska and Iowa – all four states that Trump won by double digits in 2024. With just 22 days to go, Senate Democrats’ top super PAC surprised some in its own party by investing $5 million in Kansas – a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century. “The gap is closing in Kansas,” Senate Majority PAC spokesperson Lauren French said in a statement. The investment marks a stark shift for Democratic campaign officials in Washington, who – until now – have insisted they are clear-eyed about their own realities in this midterm election. With Democrats badly outspent by the GOP, Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and his campaign arm have been careful to keep their focus strictly on the core battleground seats that are most likely to flip the Senate, according to nearly a dozen people familiar with internal discussions. But inside the party, there’s a fierce debate about how far to expand the map when Democrats are already battling for so many expensive toss-up races, with anxiety about how much to spread their limited cash without costing winnable seats. Privately, Senate Democrats had been planning to keep their limited pool of cash in what they see as must-win races in North Carolina and Georgia — even as the GOP has sharply reduced its spending in both states — as well as holding Michigan and flipping seats in Maine, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska and Texas. But now, voters’ anti-Trump backlash is driving Democrats to gamble in even redder seats. In recent days, there’s a growing sense that their party has a real shot in Kansas, in particular, where Republicans are spending almost $10 million on air to defend incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall. It’s a strategy that would have been once unthinkable for Democrats, who just weeks ago were dismissing the idea that they would seriously spend in Texas – let alone Kansas. Recent public polling showed a tied race between Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state that Trump won by 16 points two years ago. Democrats’ own internal polling in Kansas, too, showed Hamilton in a true position to compete. “Democrats expanded the map deep into GOP territory and created new opportunities to flip seats – putting us in the strongest position yet to win the Senate majority,” Schumer’s campaign arm, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, spokesperson Maeve Coyle said. “Between now and Election Day, we will keep all options on the table and pursue every strategic path to victory as resources allow.” In Kansas, Methodist megachurch pastor Hamilton has been careful to distance himself from Washington Democrats. Self-described as an “independent-minded Democrat,” Hamilton has previously told CNN he won’t support Schumer for leader. And recently, when one sitting Democratic senator offered to campaign for Hamilton, the candidate’s team turned the senator down, according to one person familiar with the discussions. Inside the cash-strapped Democratic party, there’s an increasingly fierce debate about how much to expand the Senate map — and how far to push into Trump country as the environment worsens for Republicans. With Kansas now on the map, and optimism abounds, Democrats are privately talking seriously about having a real shot of defeating Republicans in states like South Carolina, Mississippi and Nebraska. Sen. Bernie Sanders is spending some of his own money in Florida. But there’s also plenty of fear that Democrats’ decision to put money in a red state like Kansas could divert resources from a crucial battleground state like Michigan or Ohio. And among the most anxious Democrats, some are still privately pressing the party to put more money into New Hampshire or even Minnesota, two traditionally blue seats with well-known GOP candidates backed by heavy GOP spending. North Carolina Democrat Roy Cooper has been clear that the national party can’t ignore his race, either. “People are getting really excited about these expansion states. We have not won Iowa, Ohio, Texas or Alaska yet,” one Democratic operative who works on Senate races said in recent days. Some in the party, for instance, are privately raising alarms about Minnesota, with progressives like Sanders trying to direct resources there in the final days. “I worry there aren’t enough resources being invested in Minnesota …. People take it for granted as a blue state,” one Democratic operative closely tracking the Senate race there said. “You’re trying to put Maine and Texas on the map, but you also gotta play defense too.” Republicans, too, are sensing an opportunity in the state. They feel good about Republican Michele Tafoya, a well-known former NFL sideline reporter, going up against Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan. Top Senate Republicans have told donors that last-minute contributions could go far in Minnesota, according to two people familiar with the conversation – and that they believe the race winnable with more money. While Democratic officials in Minnesota aren’t publicly sounding the alarm about holding their open Senate seat, party leaders believe they have something of a built-in insurance policy: Sen. Amy Klobuchar is running for governor and will be on the top of the ticket and could help lift other Democrats over the finish line. Still, some in the party point out that Kamala Harris only won the state by 4 points two years ago and it shouldn’t be ignored this fall. The complicating factor for Democrats is money. While Democratic candidates and groups have raised record sums, Senate Republicans have benefited from even more massive spending from GOP super PACs aligned with President Donald Trump and Elon Musk. Top Democrats have been clear that they simply don’t have enough money to go after every potentially competitive seat. In the final weeks, top Senate Democrats’ mindset had been to “stay the course” in their current battlefield rather than expanding it at the last minute into places like South Carolina, according to one person granted anonymity to discuss internal conversations. “This is not the time that we need to do anything differently,” that person said, noting that top Democrats are stressing caution in the final weeks: “There’s going to be some turbulence between now and Election Day.” Even so, Senate Democrats are not dismissing the chances outright of an upset in these states. Schumer’s campaign arm has encouraged senators to play up the expanding map, including tightening races like Mississippi or South Carolina, and has told senators directly, “We don’t take options off the table,” according to one person familiar with the discussions. And Schumer has personally told donors that Mississippi’s Senate race deserves attention, another person familiar with the discussions told CNN. But campaign officials have also been clear that they can’t take their attention off the other toss-up races that they need to flip control of the Senate, or even traditionally blue seats that have seen unusual amounts of spending. “Everything feels really good right now. The question is, can that hold?” another Democratic operative working on congressional races said.

title: Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
content: A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October. That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date. Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus. The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell. The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business. Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati. The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there. His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home. Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September. Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection. Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria. On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care. We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases. However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town. Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease. But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day. Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May. The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August. But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police. It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border. Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October. Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations. Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks. Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital. By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding. Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo. He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures. The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues. The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital. Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials. Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later. Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival. "When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said. The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected. The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist. Follow us on Twitter @BBCAfrica , on Facebook at BBC Africa or on Instagram at bbcafrica More than 500 migrants have been expelled from the US to African countries, HRW says, citing US data. The patient passed through multiple cities in DR Congo, drove to Uganda and eventually flew to Kenya. The patient had been living in DR Congo, where more than 4,000 people have died from the disease this year. Kennington residents fundraise for the much-needed resource which will open on 10 October. A voter mobilisation campaign has registered huge numbers of young people but it is not clear who they are backing. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved.
